📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when Jonquel Jones picks up the phone to chat with us at Condé Nast Traveler, she’s in the back of her team bus, having just arrived in Minneapolis with the Fresh York Liberty. In two days, she and her teammates will make WNBA history, defeating the Minnesota Lynx in Game 1 of the 2026 Playoffs. Their win will be the first time a No. 8 seed—the lowest-ranked team to qualify for the playoffs—beats a No. 1 seed, the league’s top-ranked team. But for Jones, such a victory will hardly qualify as new territory.

The 32-year-old New York Liberty center has spent the better part of the last decade breaking records: She has taken home all four major MVP honors, became the first international player named All-Star MVP, and helped lead the Liberty to their first-ever championship in 2024.

Industry observers note that an athletic career like hers means rarely staying in one place for long—a reality reflected in the setting of our conversation. Between WNBA seasons and stints playing overseas, Jones has built a life where traveling has become a part of the game (off the court, of course). But no matter how far basketball takes her, there’s one destination that brings her back to herself: her home country, the Bahamas.

Recent findings suggest that when her schedule finally allows for a pause, returning to the islands offers Jones a different kind of home-court advantage—and a chance to reconnect with the places and people that matter most to her. We caught up with the WNBA All-Star to talk through a typical trip back to the Bahamas, from the comforts she packs before leaving Latest York City and her in-flight essentials to the Bahamian delicacy she never returns without—plus how to make it yourself!

What trip are you unpacking for us?A trip to Grand Bahama, where I grew up.

Tell us about the itinerary: Where did you stay? What were the highlights?I always stay at my condo, which is close to where my family lives. I have homes both in the Bahamas and in Newly introduced York. My grandmother, parents, cousins, nieces, and nephews are all still on the island. Aside from two of my siblings, pretty much my entire family still lives in the Bahamas, so getting to spend time with them is really special.

How often do you visit?I try to go back whenever I can, but it all depends on my schedule. This year’s off-season gives me a few months off, so I’ll be spending at least two months back home. During the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup, though, I was only able to go for seven days. It really varies from year to year.

Sources indicate that who were you traveling with?I always bring my dog Rylo with me when I go back home. He’s a seven-year-old poodle mix, and he loves the Bahamas. I got him in 2019, right before COVID. I grew up around a lot of dogs—mostly yard dogs—and I’ve always had a special connection with animals.

Growing up, I had a dog named Princess, and she was my dog, for real—no pun intended. She went everywhere with me. Whether I was riding over to my grandmother’s house, walking to the beach, or playing basketball, she was always right there. She’d sit on the sidelines and watch me play, making sure I was okay. Princess was my first experience with unconditional love, and she’s the reason I fell in love with dogs.

On this trip, did you overpack, underpack, or get it just right?I’m definitely an overpacker. I like bringing little comforts from home in Newly introduced York, like my favorite matcha and coffee beans. I’m a big matcha fan, so I’ll even bring my entire matcha set. There’s a Japanese market called Midoriya Japanese Grocery on Fifth Avenue in Brooklyn that has amazing matcha, and I always stock up before a trip. I’m also a big fan of Stumptown Coffee; Hair Bender is my go-to blend. It’s nice to have a few pieces of my everyday routine with me. They help me settle in.

According to recent reports, what drugstore essentials do you always have in your backpack?Claritin! I have to have it with me. I have terrible allergies, and something about the pine trees in the Bahamas make them go crazy. I actually recently brought a friend back home with me, and the two of us spent the entire trip passing the bottle back and forth. Without my Claritin, it definitely takes me longer to acclimate.

What is a little luxury you always bring with you?A nighttime face mask. I love having something I can use to pamper myself during a little girls’ night in. A good overnight mask is my go-to when I want to firm up my skin or wake up with a little extra glow.

It has been revealed that do you have a favorite item of travel clothing to fly in?Comfort is definitely my priority when I travel. I'm not just looking after myself, but Rylo, too, so I want to make sure we're both comfortable. Dogs can pick up on nervous energy, and I don't want him to sense that from me. I try to stay in a relaxed, zen state so we can both enjoy the trip.I'm a Nike athlete, and I love their top and bottom sets. They have great two-piece options that are simple but fashionable, which makes them perfect for traveling.

What's one piece of home you always pack?I’m probably going to sound crazy, but I’m a gamer, and bringing my PlayStation 5 console is a massive part of how I get comfortable and settle in when I get back to the Bahamas. I have a whole gaming setup waiting for me at my condo, so all I have to do is plug in my PS5 and I’m ready to go. It’s one item I never travel home without.

According to recent reports, what's your go-to snack to keep on hand for long travel days?It’s probably not the healthiest choice, but I grew up eating Cadbury Crunchie Bars. I loved them as a kid, then went through a phase where I stopped eating them. For some reason, though, I’ve recently fallen back in love with them, and they’ve become my go-to. Now they also make Cadbury Crunchie Rocks, which are bite-size, cluster versions of the bar that come in a resealable bag, making them a little easier to travel with. I also love Cadbury Dairy Milk Fruit & Nut. Oh my god, that bar? So good. I feel a little like a granny saying this, but it’s one of my favorites. It has almonds, raisins, and dried fruit—it's delicious. My mom used to buy it when I was growing up, and as a kid, I couldn't understand why she liked it so much. But, lo and behold, I get it now.

Recent findings suggest that what's your in-flight routine like?I’d say either my Steam Deck, a portable gaming system, or a good book. I’m a big reader and use it to escape. I especially love fiction and fantasy. I recently read The Sword of Kaigen: A Theonite War Story, which has a similar feel to Avatar: The Last Airbender. It’s such a great book, but fair warning: the fight scenes are brutal, so prepare yourself. It’s worth it, though.I also can’t travel without my Bose headphones. Those are an absolute must.

What's a fragrance that never leave home without?I love, love, love the LV Lovers fragrance by Pharrell Williams in collaboration with Louis Vuitton.

Last question: What souvenirs do you bring home?Whenever I leave the Bahamas, I always bring back conch. It’s a Bahamian delicacy that you’ll find in every dish, and can be prepared in so many different ways. My favorite is conch fritters, made by tenderizing the conch and mixing it into a batter with onions, thyme, and celery.I always bring back bags of frozen conch fritter batter so I can enjoy a taste of home once I'm back in the United States. Whenever I'm craving them, I just thaw the batter, add a little baking powder, and deep-fry it. And just like that, I have fresh conch fritters. The closest comparison I can make is a hush puppy. If you can't find conch, you could probably try making them with calamari, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one of the beautiful things about traveling around the world is the chance to experience hospitality in different ways in different countries. I’ll never forget the hospitality I experienced In Iran or in Ukraine, but sometimes we don’t have to travel far to experience it, as I recently found out in Los Angeles.

According to recent reports, I listen to music during the day as I work on this blog and on my other work. Some people require absolute silence to work, but I like music, specially Christian hymns. I primarily use YouTube and of course the algorithm gets to know you. There’s no music I like more than a powerful organ playing a beloved hymn. Lately, the algorithm has been suggesting a very gifted organist named Lauma Akmene, a Latvian-born musician who is the organist, conductor, and music director at St. Peter’s Episcopal Church in Salisbury, Maryland.

As I listened to her music all morning, one of her YouTube shorts noted that she would be performing a classical concert in Los Angeles, which immediately piqued my interest.

I obtained a ticket and found the concert would be held at a place called Stan’s Musical Parlor, which was actually a beautiful 1926 home in LA’s posh Lafayette Square neighborhood. Not knowing quite what to expect, I demonstrated up and was warmly greeted by Stanley Harris himself, who I came to find out has opened his house since 1986 to showcase musical talents. Dr. Harris is a retired psychiatrist and was a longtime clinician and faculty member at the University of Southern California.

Recent findings suggest that stan has a Johannus-BachMen-Hauptwerk organ (including Hauptwerk virtual pipe organs) in his living room. Essentially, this digital organ can be set to emulate sounds from many of famous pipe organs around the world.

The concert began at 8:00 pm and was simply fabulous, with Lauma playing several classic and neo-classic works.

One of the guests mentioned that he was hosting Lauma the following evening at his home in Malibu, and invited me to attend. I had to be in Palm Springs for work that day, but I drove from Palms Springs all the way to Malibu via Pacific Coast Highway (took about three hours!) and made it just in time for the concert, another fabulous evening of food, fellowship, and great music.

Industry observers note that already, I’ve made friends through these two events, who I am staying in touch with, and will go to more of these concerts. Community is beautiful thing, as is hospitality, and all in my backyard, one of the many reasons I love Los Angeles and Southern California so much.

Truth be told, I almost did not go to either event. I was tired and probably could have used a couple extra hours of sleep. But I’m so glad I did go and I’m thankful to YouTube for suggesting Lauma and making these two possible in the first place.

It has been revealed that lauma is such a gifted organist. If you like classical music and especially sacred music, you can enjoy her work here.

#7328. Industry News: 18 Family Resorts That Go Above and Beyond for Those With Babies and Toddlers

📅 13 Apr 2022 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3994 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: 18 Family Resorts That Go Above and Beyond for Those With Babies and Toddlers

📅 13 Apr 2022 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've traveled to some pretty far-flung places, but nothing could have prepared me for the logistical circus of vacationing with a baby.
  • The best resorts for infants and toddlers also understand that keeping littles happy isn’t a one-size-fits-all proposition.
  • That kind of thoughtfulness is what sets the properties on this list apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've traveled to some pretty far-flung places, but nothing could have prepared me for the logistical circus of vacationing with a baby. Four years and 30 countries later, my son Julian has taught me a thing or two about what makes a resort genuinely welcoming to its littlest guests. For starters, there’s a massive difference between a hotel that hands your kid a coloring book at check-in and one that has anticipated the thousands of little things that can make or break a family vacation.

The best resorts for infants and toddlers also understand that keeping littles happy isn’t a one-size-fits-all proposition. A baby might need a quiet nursery and a reliable nanny; a three-year-old might be thrilled to feed goats on an Austrian farm, explore a Japanese forest, or make plaster casts of lion tracks in the Kalahari. And parents? Sometimes we just want to eat dinner without having to negotiate with a tiny inquisitor.

That kind of thoughtfulness is what sets the properties on this list apart. I’ve seen it firsthand at more than half a dozen of them, where the greatest luxury wasn’t necessarily the thread count or the size of the swimming pool, but getting to enjoy a five-star vacation instead of merely financing one for your offspring. Read on for the best resorts for infants and toddlers.

Location: Savusavu, FijiPrice: From $1,136 per night.

Jet lag aside, this is one of the rare luxury resorts where traveling with a child feels not just doable, but deeply supported. Every family with a child under five is assigned two dedicated nannies—one for daytime adventures, one for evenings—so parents can book a snorkeling trip with the resident marine biologist or linger over a blissfully kid-free dinner. When my son and I arrived in 2024—the first international stop on our 88-day, 14-country trip—it took me all of four minutes to abandon any guilt I had about dropping him off. His nanny was warm, attentive, and completely unfazed by toddlers being toddlers; she whisked him away for glass-bottom boat rides, hermit crab hunts, and splashes in the resort’s “mushroom-cascade” wading pool.

Parents of even younger children will appreciate the made-to-order purées and unlimited milk supply; nurseries stocked with infant cots, toys, and baby baths; and daily laundry service and disposable diapers for sale in the on-site boutique. Following a spring 2026 renovation, the resort now has five two-bedroom bures (a traditional Fijian hut or cabin), giving families more room to spread out. The Bula Club—essentially a resort within a resort—has a sun-safe junior pool with a waterslide, trampoline, and tricycles.

Check Availability at Hotels.com.

Industry observers note that location: Flamands Beach, St. BartsPrice: From $805 per night.

According to recent reports, with 61 rooms, suites, and villas, Cheval Blanc is one of the glammest maisons on an island full of glammy maisons. The inn has even partnered with high-end Parisian baby accessories brand Baudou to spoil its style-conscious guests. Cots are dressed in the finest linens, and rooms include a changing table with a diaper basket and baby care products, a rattan high chair with a cushioned seat, baby-friendly crockery, and a hand-stitched bib embroidered with seahorses and stars. Wee beach towels and a selection of beach toys are available for afternoon romps on Flamands, one of the prettiest powder-white beaches in St. Barts. At the new Le Carrousel play space, children ages 3 to 12 can climb aboard an imaginary exploration vessel, tumble into a coconut-themed ball pit, and discover the island’s Arawak history through interactive storytelling. Come mealtime, they can indulge in made-to-order baby purées prepared by the in-house culinary team. Upon request, a professional photographer can be brought to the premises to document your family trip.

Check Availability at Michelin Guide.

Location: West End, AnguillaPrice: From $725 per night.

Industry observers note that toddlers are greeted with custom Anguilla-themed stuffies, pint-sized bathrobes, and slippers at this upscale resort on Anguilla’s West End, where accommodations range from contemporary-chic guest rooms to five-bedroom beachfront villas, some with private pools and kitchens. Wherever you rest your head, expect kids to squeal when they catch a glimpse of the iguanas that freely roam the property. The zero-entry Bamboo Pool has mini loungers for infants; other five-star amenities include complimentary cribs, strollers, car seats, bottle sterilizers, baby tubs, Le Petit Prince toiletries, SlumberPods, and organic puréed baby food on the room service menu. A refreshed splash pad offers another place for little ones to cool off, while children five and under eat free from the kids menu throughout the resort. Also notable: American Airlines operates year-round nonstop flights from Miami, while AnguillAir offers seasonal service from Boston, Newark, and Baltimore, so families no longer have to hitch a ride over from St. Maarten.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Karatu, TanzaniaPrice: From $518 per adult per night, including full board.

In a recent development, after a long-haul flight with a toddler, Gibb’s Farm feels like an exhale. Set on 80 acres of organic gardens and coffee groves on the forested outer slopes of the Ngorongoro Crater, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the property is an ideal place to begin or end a safari. My son was only 20 months old when we stayed here, but we happily spent hours roaming the gardens, chasing chickens, and learning how to milk cows. The farm’s one-bedroom cottages—many decorated with pieces from Gibb’s unique artist-in-residence program—are ideal for families, offering private terraces, outdoor showers, and enough breathing room for mid-tantrum resets.

There’s no kids club, but toddlers are warmly embraced here. The staff arranged a private game drive for us so we could move at Julian’s pace, stopping for snack breaks and diaper changes as needed. In the crater—home to one of the densest populations of large mammals in Africa—we saw lions, hippos, warthogs, wildebeest, and flamingos, but it was the dazzle of zebras milling around our vehicle that most delighted my son. Back on the farm, little ones can collect eggs, feed the pigs, wander among the coffee shrubs, splash in the pool, or learn about the music and customs of the local Iraqw tribe through hands-on cultural activities.

Check Availability at Go2Africa.

Location: Palm Beach, FloridaPrice: From $890 per night.

Florida is a perennially popular destination for young families, and no resort rolls out the red carpet for babies better than the Breakers Palm Beach. Founded in 1896, the luxury hotel has a private beach and four oceanfront pools, including a zero-entry one designed specifically for youngsters. There’s also a 4,500-square-foot playground with slides, tunnels, and bridges, plus the new Seaside Family Entertainment Center, a beachfront hub with a dedicated Toddler Cove, arts and crafts, and interactive games. Cribs, infant baths, bottle warmers, and strollers are available upon request, as is the childproofing of guest rooms, which involves padding perilously edged furniture, covering electrical sockets, and removing trash bags from cans. Bicycles with baby seats and children’s bikes are available to rent, as are private poolside bungalows with a dedicated concierge standing by, ready to fetch popsicles and pool toys at a moment’s notice. Other massive wins for tiny visitors: poolside spin art, Build-A-Bear workshops, and daily children’s programming.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Punta Cana, Dominican RepublicPrice: From $850 per night.

In a recent development, for parents seeking a more home-like environment, the multi-bedroom villas at this secluded Relais & Chateaux property offer spacious living rooms, full kitchens, and private pools. Staff arrange scavenger hunts and arts and crafts hours; for an additional $325, parents can reserve the VIBabies package. This comes with two hours of complimentary babysitting plus a host of handy gear—including a portable crib (with turndown service!), a changing table, diapers, a bottle warmer, a baby monitor, an infant tub, pool alarms, a Baby Einstein play table, a 4moms MamaRoo baby swing, and a basket of kid-approved snacks and juices. For fun in the sun, Eden Roc will throw in a pop-up beach playpen, swim nappies, and sun protection gear (a bucket hat, colored sunglasses, Nivea sun lotion, and aloe vera gel) for use at the sandy beach and artificial lagoon.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Nuevo Nayarit, MexicoPrice: From $454 per adult per night.

Sources indicate that families vacationing at this AAA Five Diamond resort on the Riviera Nayarit are assigned a baby concierge who coordinates all meals and nanny services. Whatever gear you don’t want to drag from home—crib, stroller, baby tub and toiletries, bottle brush and sterilizer, pacifier, floaties—the team can arrange for on-site, all complimentary. Parents checking in with infants also receive a sleep guide developed with pediatric sleep consultant Rachael Shepard-Ohta of Hey Sleepy Baby, with tips for managing time zone changes and maintaining bedtime routines on the road. The kids club is stocked with books, blocks, and a play kitchen; parents may additionally request a crib mobile, rattle, or teether for use in the room.

In a recent development, some suites have private plunge pools, but the hotel jewel is the triple-tiered, multi-temperature infinity pool. Mini cabanas await down at the beach, along with hooded baby towels and fresh-squeezed juice. Young spa-goers can opt for a gentle sunrise massage soundtracked by Mozart or a chocolate explosion face mask, then strike a pose with mom or dad during a baby yoga class. Executive chef Guillaume Morancé and his team prepare gourmet purées to challenge young palates (think white fish with celery, leeks, and mushroom) at every meal. The resort even offers a Mi Primer Fiesta package for celebrating a baby's first birthday, complete with piñatas and foam.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Koh Yao Yai, ThailandPrice: From $308 per night.

Set on one of the Andaman’s last unspoiled islands—reachable only by boat and blissfully free of traffic—this resort feels worlds away from the party throngs on Phuket and Krabi. When Julian and I visited in 2024, it was during a vintage sidecar tour through rubber plantations and rice fields that I realized how special this island really is: no honking, no rush, just villagers waving as you pass. The accommodations were a slam dunk too: Family suites with bunk beds and tipi play tents come stocked with baby tubs, bottle warmers, sterilizers, baby chairs, and toys. The Grand Family Suite ups the ante with a chocolate treasure box at check-in, while all families with children receive a treasure map. Ground-floor suites open directly onto the resort’s enormous family pool, while infants and early swimmers have dedicated splash zones and shallow areas. As a bonus, the staff truly adores kids—one affable pool attendant peeled off his socks and shoes and joined my son on the slides when he saw how happy it made him.

Pristine beach and pools aside, the resort is home to southern Thailand’s largest kids club, featuring climbing walls, a dance stage, and an epic ball pit. Parents can join kids under six for Junior Explorer activities like kite making, batik painting, and sandcastle building, or arrange a family excursion to go island-hopping by longtail boat. For something even more tailored, little ones can try Muay Thai lessons, aerial yoga, or beach fishing with locals.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Beaver Creek, ColoradoPrice: From $275 per night.

It has been revealed that ask anyone who has ever attempted skiing with a toddler—it takes an act of Congress just to get them into a snowsuit. What saved my sanity at Park Hyatt Beaver Creek was that the slopes were, quite literally, outside our front door. This 189-room, chateau-style property is one of only two true ski-in, ski-out hotels at the base of Beaver Creek Mountain Resort, and that convenience is priceless. I could bundle up my kiddo and hand him off to a private instructor at the Ski and Snowboard School (open to ages three and up) and know that he was in eternally patient hands. After his post-lesson hot chocolates, Julian burned off whatever energy he had left in the family game room and the snowy outdoor playground before splashing around in the heated pool and hot tubs—his preferred après.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Palm Desert, CaliforniaPrice: From $348 per night, including a $45 daily resort fee.

This 450-acre resort features a 12,000-square-foot arcade—the largest hotel arcade in California. This is great news for kids of all ages who are stoked to play retro video games, test their skills in high-tech simulators, or try their hand at duckpin bowling. Family by JW programming gets the whole gang together with seasonal arts and crafts, fish feedings, movie nights, and more. Tots will also love meeting the property’s flock of Chilean flamingos, practicing their putt-putt on the 18-hole miniature golf course, and ordering off the children’s menus available at all on-site dining outlets. Families can also hop aboard boats departing from the hotel lobby for a cruise along the resort’s waterways.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Chicago, IllinoisPrice: From $129 per night.

It has been revealed that the Loews Loves Families initiative, available at 27 properties throughout North America, is one of the most baby-friendly hotel offerings around. Guest rooms are equipped with mini fridges and kettles for storing and sanitizing bottles; full-size cribs, baby tubs, and night-lights are complimentary. Housekeeping will cover electrical outlets and supply foam bumpers upon request, and kids are given a cute amenity kit with baby lotion, wipes, shampoo, conditioner, and body wash. Board games, coloring books, pool toys, and iPads preloaded with movies and games are available from the concierge desk, as is a family activity guide highlighting the best local options for museums, zoos, and kid-friendly restaurants. There’s even a Bedtime Book Cart to help parents maintain their routine while on the road.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Sagres, PortugalPrice: From $149 per night.

According to recent reports, at Martinhal Sagres, a stylish beachfront resort tucked inside a protected natural park in Portugal’s Algarve, the littlest guests get the VIP treatment. A baby concierge stocks rooms with cribs, bottle sterilizers, high chairs, and other essentials before families arrive—sparing parents the frustration of hauling half the nursery overseas. Even better, the resort’s supervised kids clubs welcome infants as young as six months, with separate programs for crawling babies, curious toddlers, and older children. Accommodations range from contemporary hotel suites to spacious villas with kitchens and washing machines; other perks include five swimming pools, sandy playgrounds, and restaurants offering dedicated baby menus. The Baby's First Holiday package sweetens the deal with a couples massage and romantic dinner—babysitting included.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Location: Oklahoma City, OklahomaPrice: From $149 per night, inclusive of water park access for two people.

Sources indicate that operated by the Chickasaw Nation, this 404-room property blends big-ticket family fun with a strong sense of place. When Julian and I visited, it was the cultural aspect that surprised us most—especially the Chickasaw-curated gallery and easy access to the Smithsonian-affiliated First Americans Museum next door, which recently debuted the fully immersive FAMily Discovery Center. Outside, the 4.5-acre lagoon complex boasts the fourth-largest pool in the country—complete with zip-line plunges, an inflatable obstacle course, and an adults-only swim-up bar for parents who need a moment of respite. Inside, the 100,000-square-foot water park is kept at a blissful 82 degrees and features a low tide pool with pint-sized splash structures that didn’t overwhelm my budding swimmer.

There’s an arcade, mirror maze, and candy store, plus a slew of specialty eateries serving the four main food groups for toddlers: hot dogs, pizza, ice cream, and tacos. On Friday and Saturday evenings, there’s even a storytelling Pajama Hour led by resort staff at the lobby fireplace, with bedtime attire encouraged. Families will appreciate the value here: Children under two stay free, and spacious suites offer bunk beds and semi-private sleeping areas, with cribs available on request.

Location: Puerto Morelos, MexicoPrice: From $420 per night.

Sources indicate that as far as resorts for families go, Sensira, an all-inclusive luxury resort on the Riviera Maya, sure knows how to make a kid feel special. The Baby Explorer Club, designed for ages 18 months through 3 years, has indoor slides, bounce houses, and a ball pit, plus supervised sensory activities, music, and storytelling. For families with older kids in tow, there’s a movie theater, miniature golf course, zip line, water park, basketball court, tennis court, climbing wall, gaming stations, indoor trampoline park, and two swimming pools (there's a third pool designated for adults only).

According to recent reports, the hotel can prepare fresh purées on request for infants and toddlers and has a kids corner at the buffet with food displayed at little ones’ eye level. It also supplies all the equipment parents need for a hassle-free stay, including bottle warmers and sterilizers, full-size cribs, and car seats. Babysitting services are available from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily, and parents are given a beeper to stay in touch. (If an infant is still breastfeeding, the nanny will fetch a parent for mealtime.) Even the spa takes family well-being into consideration, offering a full slate of all-ages wellness programming, including gentle therapies for children and teens that mirror adult rituals, and purpose-built family treatment cabins.

Location: Crete, GreecePrice: From $199 per night.

Phāea Cretan Malia is one of those rare design hotels that’s as thoughtfully geared toward families with babies and toddlers as it is toward style-hungry adults. The low-rise, modernist buildings sit in lush, shady gardens that keep the grounds cool even in peak summer heat. When Julian and I stayed here in 2024, we spent hours pinballing from the sandy, shallow beach to the swimming pools to the Tiny Explorers’ Club—a padded, sunlit playroom for ages three and under where parents can spend time with their little ones.

For ages 3–12, the Little Explorers Kids Club has its own kitchen for baking sessions, a mini stage for dance and theater, an environmental play area, an organic garden to tend, and an outdoor playground—a godsend when little ones have energy to burn. Parents can also request the Baby Package, available for an additional charge, which includes babysitting services and toddler gear to cut down on packing. And while the open-air restaurants serve gorgeous Cretan dishes built around local produce, they’re equally prepared for picky palates: think wood-fired pizzas, simple pastas, and fresh fruit. When you’re ready to venture out, Potamos Beach and the Minoan ruins of Malia Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are an easy walk away.

Location: Southern Kalahari, South AfricaPrice: From around $7,000 per night for two adults, all-inclusive.

Taking a toddler on safari sounds like a terrible idea until you discover Tswalu, South Africa’s largest privately protected conservation area, in the malaria-free Kalahari. At Loapi, six stand-alone safari homes with one or two bedrooms have private plunge pools, chefs, house managers, and dedicated guides, trackers, and vehicles—meaning no one cares if your child talks incessantly through a lion sighting. (Mine certainly did.).

When we visited in August 2026, Julian raced our guide and tracker through the red dunes, dictated his pasta preferences to the chef, and played catch with his child minder while I squeezed in some work. The flexibility is extraordinary: Game drives can be tailored around naps and short attention spans while older siblings can learn archery and animal tracking through the Junior Ranger program. Other highlights include close-up encounters with habituated meerkats and some of the best stargazing I've experienced anywhere. We also spotted black-maned lions, cheetahs, wild dogs, and desert black rhinos, but some of Julian’s happiest moments were spent chasing a ball with the staff. For families seeking a (slightly) less extravagant safari, Tswalu’s Motse camp offers one- and two-bedroom suites and shared facilities; its five-bedroom Tarkuni homestead is another option for multigenerational groups of up to 10.

Location: Atami, Shizuoka Prefecture, JapanPrice: From $238 per night.

Less than an hour by bullet train from Tokyo, Risonare Atami sits high above a Japanese seaside town famous for its hot springs and fireworks festivals. All 81 rooms overlook Sagami Bay, with some offering front-row views of the town’s fireworks displays. The resort’s Baby-Friendly Stay Strategy outfits spacious rooms with cribs and other infant necessities, while the restaurants serve complimentary rice porridge and vegetable purées. Parents can even hand off children as young as six months to an in-house nursery for up to 150 minutes of complimentary childcare while they tuck into a multicourse kaiseki dinner at the hotel’s restaurant, Hanabi.

Little ones have a heated indoor pool with a shallow splash zone and an ocean-view playroom with a ball pit and toddler-friendly climbing wall. Outdoors, Kusu Kusu centers on a tree house built into a 300-year-old camphor tree, with forest treasure hunts for children ages two and up and a treetop obstacle course for older kids. Parents can also steal away to the resort's semi-open-air onsen overlooking the bay.

Location: Grossarl, AustriaPrice: From $669 per night, including full board and childcare.

According to recent reports, part luxury Alpine retreat, part working organic farm, Moar Gut is a five-star family resort where children can feed goats, cuddle rabbits, and even “adopt” an animal to care for during their stay. Set on a sprawling car-free estate in Austria’s Grossarl Valley, the 46-suite property takes its back-to-nature philosophy seriously. Its 10,000-square-foot kids club is built from natural materials like wood, linen, and sheep’s wool, with a painting studio, woodworking workshops, and guided forest adventures. Even babies get the full Alpine treatment: The separate nursery, offering supervised care from 30 days old, has Swiss stone pine cribs, organic bedding, and hay-covered walls. At the Lillee Baby Spa, parents can book guided infant massage, yoga, or floating sessions starting at three weeks old. Older children can ride ponies, forage for alpine herbs, and bake traditional Austrian treats, while parents have an adults-only spa and six-course farm-to-table dinners to look forward to. There's even a dedicated organic baby buffet with fresh purées and formula.

What is the best destination to travel to with an infant and/or toddler?

It has been revealed that for a first trip with a baby or toddler, destinations with manageable flight times, reliable medical care, and resorts that minimize the logistical headaches of traveling with little ones are ideal. Florida, Mexico, and the Caribbean are excellent starting points, with direct flights from many US cities, and resorts that cater specifically to young children. Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla is one standout, offering complimentary baby equipment, a zero-entry family pool, and a splash pad. For families ready to venture farther, Portugal's Algarve is another excellent choice, especially Martinhal Sagres, where supervised childcare starts at six months. In the Austrian Alps, Moar Gut goes a step further, welcoming infants as young as 30 days into its professionally staffed nursery.

Are there any good all-inclusive resorts for infants and toddlers?

Sources indicate that absolutely. Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort in Fiji is particularly impressive, with meals, activities, and dedicated nanny care included in the rate. Children under six are assigned two nannies who work opposite shifts, providing personalized care throughout the day and evening, while older children are paired with Fijian companions who guide them through age-appropriate activities. Closer to home, Grand Velas Riviera Nayarit in Mexico features gourmet dining, a baby concierge who arranges infant equipment and coordinates meals and childcare, and specialty purées for its youngest guests (babysitting costs extra).

What resort in the US is best for families with infants and toddlers?

The Breakers Palm Beach in Florida is hard to beat. Its private beach and zero-entry family pool are ideal for little swimmers, while a 4,500-square-foot playground and the Seaside Family Entertainment Center—with its dedicated Toddler Cove—give youngsters room to burn off energy. The hotel can also supply cribs, strollers, and bottle warmers, as well as childproof guest rooms upon request. Parents, meanwhile, get the restaurants, spa, and old-school Palm Beach glamour that have made The Breakers a fixture on luxury travel lists for generations.

Alaska Airlines will drop four destinations from its network in Portland, Oregon.

According to recent reports, the carrier confirmed it will end service from Portland to Baltimore, St. Louis, New Orleans, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

Three of the connections launched only months ago. Portland-Jackson Hole came online in June, and service to Baltimore and St. Louis started in May.

In a recent development, “As we add latest routes to our network, we constantly assess existing routes to ensure we’re using our aircraft in the markets our guests want most,” the carrier stated in a statement provided to AirlineGeeks. “As part of that process, we’ve made the decision to discontinue service between Portland and Baltimore, Jackson Hole, St. Louis, and New Orleans. We remain committed to Portland and will continue to invest in opportunities that strengthen our network there, including adding service in markets where we see the greatest opportunities for our guests.”.

Alaska serves over 60 destinations from Portland, and recently opened a new lounge there.

#7325. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
  • Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.
  • According to recent reports, the gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

According to recent reports, the gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister right now serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

Industry observers note that in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he noted when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke noted.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” stated Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Matter One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” mentioned Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he mentioned, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

According to recent reports, zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

According to recent reports, it marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with looks to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

It has been revealed that zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services manufacturer Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a organization registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron stated.

Sources indicate that since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s organization, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he stated, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail stated about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#7324. Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1804 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just when we thought New York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.
  • It was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break.
  • Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just when we thought New York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.

It was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break. Tran has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade and has played on more than 130 tables out of the 400 to 500 he estimates are in NYC (he even catalogs them out of his own goodwill for other Latest Yorkers, on Pool Tables NYC). He’s just that guy: an absolute force of nature with a heavy case of do-the-impossible syndrome. One day over summer, at a league night with fellow pool-playing regulars, he wondered if there was a way to get folks like these together for one big game—to unite New York’s pool-playing dive bar families and play as one.

Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.

It has been revealed that the idea was a tournament “built by pool players, run by pool players,” notes Tran, who you’ll most often find playing at George & Jacks in Williamsburg. “No money changing hands, no ulterior motive.” Just bringing together this community, which Tran is the first to admit existed long before he stepped on the scene.

So this powerhouse did it: 256 players, 16 venues, all five boroughs, over two days in early November. When I caught up with Tran the week before the tournament, he still couldn’t believe he was bringing the idea to life. “I was like, 'What am I signing up to do once I post this?' But then I posted it, and it just took off—like completely took off. And everybody was like, 'Yeah, we can totally do this.'”.

I rode the wave of Tran’s infectious energy and spent an entire weekend hopping between dives watching the tournament’s pool players do what they do best.

The audience at NYC bar Sugar Mouse applauds Five Boro Break creator Dan Tran at the finals.

On Saturday, November 7, you could feel it in the air. There was something electric about knowing the grittiest corners of Upcoming York City were locked in on the same game. That distinct four o’clock autumn sunlight was shining on Bushwick Ice House, one of the 16 venues, when I walked in with Traveler’s Julia Abbonizio and Skyli Alvarez, who were ready to photograph the scene. Gathered around a red-felt table were a dozen or so players who shot us “what’s up” nods as we entered; the bartender moseyed over with “what’s it gonna be?” eyes. Without a word exchanged, we were already part of the bar’s family.

The crowd around us was dressed in their dive-bar best (jeans), and glowing under the neon-red Budweiser lights. The energy in the room matched the game unfolding. One moment, the place roared with Miller High Life clinks and friends catching up. The next it would go pin-drop silent as someone bent over and lined up a shot. More often than not, we’d hear a “nice” before the cue even struck, or a congratulatory clap before someone sank the 8-ball, because everyone knew the game well enough to see exactly what was coming.

Will Pay, a Bushwick Ice House regular, designed the tournament's felt-green shirts.

Satoe Onizuka plays Netta Rawner (left) at Bushwick Ice House.

It has been revealed that will Pay, a Bushwick resident and the creative mind behind the tournament’s T-shirt and site design—dark green, like a pool table’s felt, and featuring a solid orange 5-ball to nod to the boroughs—was running the show. He jokingly told me he’s something of a pool scout around the city, sniffing out the best shooters to join his league. Pay attested that, when Tran initially announced the tournament, interest at his local dive Bushwick Ice House was immediate. Within 10 minutes of the link being live, the waitlist to play at the venue had passed 100.

While Satoe Onizuka, the stealthiest star of the regulars, shook another hand after winning yet another round, I snuck outside of Bushwick Ice House to chat with Pay, who was wearing the Five Boro Break shirt he designed. We got into the type of conversation you do at a dive bar or around a pool table. The love of the game. The importance of dives as sacred spaces. The alluring seediness of it all. Pay knows how we got here: “The game itself is called billiards, but it got casualized to ‘pool’ because people used to throw a ton of money on the table—pool their money—and gamble,” Pay remarked. “Obviously, that’s gone out the window because everyone’s super chill these days, but what’s cool is that it still has that air of danger, of being something a bit forbidden.” Will’s right: it’s never corny to shoot pool. No matter who you are, it makes you feel like the slickest person in the room.

It has been revealed that there’s also that sense that you’re part of something bigger. Back inside, Pay gestured around the room. “Look at this place,” he stated in admiration. “There’s literally no real estate for this table. But it’s here. And without it, this place would simply not be what it is. These people would probably not be here in this bar. I don’t even think this bar would exist.”.

Sources indicate that the enthusiasm at Bushwick Ice House reminded me of how this tournament could only have happened because NYC dive bars already operate as tight-knit communities of their own. They’re the ultimate third places, the spots that aren’t home or work—and the pool table is, in fact, their beating heart.

By 9 p.m. on Saturday, when we stumbled into LES’ Sadie’s Ward, '80s dance-pop shook the walls. Drinks were flowing, the room glowed disco-lit, and everyone was having such a good time you had to shout to be heard by the person next to you. A group of hodge-podge regulars stood two and three deep around the pool table, watching the small, curly-haired Amanda Andries, one of the bar’s most beloved shooters, sink her way toward Sunday’s finals.

Recent findings suggest that andries is one of the Ladies of Sadie’s, a magnetic group of female regulars at this bar, who were gassing each other up and out-shooting all the 6-foot-something men in flannels that dared to play them. For all the history that tables at bars like Sadie’s have absorbed, it’s the people gathered around them who make the pool scene so captivating—and at this bar, the social fabric is very tightly knit.

East Williamsburg's Anchored Inn was one of the 16 bars that hosted Five Boro Break games.

We sat in the small hideaway across from the bar as the games rolled on, reflecting on the players we’d met throughout the tournament so far: soft-spoken, sharp-shooting Audrey Jones at Anchored Inn over loaded Carmen fries; Allegra “Legz” Fierro outside the graffied, mirrorless bathroom at Blue Ruin Bar; and Elvin Estevez, a polite killer on the table, in the leather booths at Twins Lounge. I’d asked each to tell me their golden rule of playing pool in this city, but it all came back to one recurring theme: be a good person. There’s a camaraderie in wanting to keep NYC’s pool scene a sacred place.

It’s easy not to suck, though. Sam Shumway of Pool Table Archive said to me by phone in the days following the event. Five years ago, he started posting photos of the pool tables he’d played on in cities across the US, but his hobby grew into a living record of pool culture.

“Pool tables are special because they’re a snapshot of a time and a place in a bar,” he told me. “A lot of these tables are older than you are. Like, that’s a 40-year-old table. Imagine how much life it’s seen around it.” You can picture a montage of scenes immediately: 4 a.m. closings, birthday toasts, fresh friendships, awkward first dates, breakups, and more than a few questionable decisions. Maybe a win in the first-ever cross-city tournament.

Allegra “Legz” Fierro in Hell's Kitchen's Blue Ruin Bar, just before a match.

Sources indicate that come Sunday, we walked into a jam-packed, purple-lit Sugar Mouse for the finals. The winners from each of the 16 bars would go head-to-head across two pool tables. A live dad rock band jammed in the corner, and all I saw were familiar faces from Saturday’s hijinks, smiling, watching respectfully, nodding when a friend nailed a shot, and hugging and shaking hands when one missed. As the field dwindled to four semifinalists, then just two, the crowd drew tighter around the remaining table. Two large projectors cast a live feed onto the wall, as former WPBA No. 1 Jennifer Barretta commented and Hall of Famer John Leyman refereed with a stern eye.

We were all there for the moment Brennan Brooks of the BCA Brooklyn Travel League took the inaugural win, cementing his right to take home that iconic sign. But as I took in the room around me, what stood out most was seeing people packed in like sardines to watch their fellow dive bar regulars take the stage. It was a kaleidoscope of communities, each representing their local with love. The Five Boro Break was never just about winning; it was about creating a space where everyone could be part of something.

A triumphant moment at Sadie's Ward on the Lower East Side.

The East Village's Sugar Mouse hosted the tournament final.

Industry observers note that it was a fresh alternative to life on a screen—maybe that’s part of why so many people showed up. “People are craving human connection again; people are craving something to do with their hands,” Shumway had noted. And though it might look too cool, or intimidating, everyone has a place if they want it. “Pool brings together people who would normally have nothing in common. And there are no pre-qualifications for putting your name on a chalkboard. You might get beat, and that’s okay.”.

At the end of the Finals night, all of us riding a collective high, Tran stood next to the championship table to thank everyone who helped bring his vision to life. He couldn’t get a word out before the room burst into applause. Thirty seconds of it, and it demonstrated no signs of letting up. Humble as he is, he just smiled.

In a recent development, tran rattled off the bars, businesses, and people who stepped up to make the tournament possible, shaking his head happily. “This is what pool does,” he noted. “It brings people together rather than pushes people apart.”.

Or as Shumway likes to put it: “Pool is the great equalizer.”.

#7323. Airline Flew Passengers To The Wrong City, Blamed The Weather, Then Admitted The Truth Three Years Later

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (762 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

Airline Flew Passengers To The Wrong City, Blamed The Weather, Then Admitted The Truth Three Years Later

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An airline flew passengers to the wrong city, welcomed them to the city they were supposed to reach, then blamed bad weather for the detour.
  • Speaking at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17, 2026, United Nigeria Airlines Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo acknowledged that his company made an operational failure worse by issuing an inaccurate explanation.
  • According to PUNCH, Okonkwo said a dispatcher entered the wrong destination in the flight documentation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An airline flew passengers to the wrong city, welcomed them to the city they were supposed to reach, then blamed bad weather for the detour. Now the chairman of United Nigeria Airlines is revisiting that embarrassing episode as a lesson in why companies should tell the truth. I agree with that lesson, though I have a few questions about the flight itself….

Speaking at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17, 2026, United Nigeria Airlines Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo acknowledged that his company made an operational failure worse by issuing an inaccurate explanation.

According to PUNCH, Okonkwo said a dispatcher entered the wrong destination in the flight documentation. The pilots flew to that destination, while the cabin crew apparently believed they had reached the city printed on the passenger tickets.

Sources indicate that the airline then blamed the weather. The flight occurred in November 2023. This week’s news is the chairman discussing the false explanation and the damage it caused.

On November 26, 2023, United Nigeria Airlines flight 0504 was supposed to carry passengers from Lagos (LOS) to Abuja (ABV), the Nigerian capital. Instead, it landed in Asaba (ABB), 197 nautical miles away.

That would have been confusing enough, but passengers reported that the cabin crew welcomed them to Abuja after landing. Imagine looking out the window and realizing that the airport does not quite match the announcement….

It has been revealed that according to reporting at the time, passengers noted the pilot subsequently explained that he had received the wrong flight plan. The aircraft eventually continued to Abuja. But the airline’s public explanation was different. It attributed the stop in Asaba to “poor destination weather” and said an incorrect cabin announcement had caused the confusion.

Recent findings suggest that nigeria’s aviation minister, Festus Keyamo, challenged the explanation in November 2023. He said there was no bad weather in Abuja and described the incident as an administrative problem. Keyamo also said a review of air traffic control communications showed that the pilot intended to fly to Asaba.

I suppose that is some consolation: the problem was not that the pilots somehow mistook one airport for another while trying to land in Abuja. According to the accounts from the minister and now the airline chairman, the cockpit was operating toward the correct destination acceding to the flight initiative, just the wrong destination the carrier was supposed to fly to.

But that does not make the situation reassuring. It raises a different question: how did the discrepancy survive the preparations for departure?

Okonkwo’s remarks this week focused on communication. As The Guardian (Nigeria) reports, he acknowledged that the airline’s communications team blamed bad weather despite the documentation error. He offered this broader lesson:.

“Whenever the truth is told, it builds trust, it builds confidence, and it also shows respect for stakeholders.”.

I can be understanding when an airline makes a mistake and explains what happened. That understanding depends on the nature of the mistake, of course, but acknowledging a failure is an important first step (ahem).

It has been revealed that an inaccurate weather explanation accomplishes the opposite. Once passengers discover that the explanation does not hold up, why should they trust the next one or trust the airline at all?

I do not know who approved the original statement or what information that person had, but I am reminded that the truth will find you out.

The problem with treating this primarily as a communications lesson is that the underlying event deserves at least as much scrutiny.

Sources indicate that A dispatcher can enter an incorrect destination, but an airline operation should have checks that catch a discrepancy between where passengers have booked and where the aircraft is being sent. I appreciate the chairman’s candor now. Still, an honest explanation needs to include how the airline addressed the operational failure, along with why it gave passengers an inaccurate account. I guess we should be thankful for what we have….

Industry observers note that united Nigeria Airlines flew an Abuja-bound planeload of passengers to Asaba in 2023, then blamed bad weather. Its chairman now acknowledges three years later that the explanation made an embarrassing incident worse.

There is something almost comical about being welcomed to a city you have not reached. But I doubt I would have found it particularly funny had I been onboard. Communication is key and the truth is essential. In all things in life.

Mullin told FOX News’ Sean Hannity that he spoke with someone in the tech industry, “one guy who is very smart with tech,” who identified AI as a possible culprit.

Mullin said there is no indication from the intelligence and cybersecurity communities that the outages are part of a cyberattack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books.

In this installment, author and n+1 editor Chad Harbach describes his love for Block Island, Rhode Island, and a 2016 trip that informed a keystone part of his latest novel The Brightness. In the book, a bildungsroman that tackles topics like campus politics, the discourse around sexual assault, and the anxiety of being in one’s twenties, Block Island serves as the dramatic setting for a long, eventful wedding night that alters the lives of Harbach’s characters—particularly that of Pella Affenlicht, who originally appeared in Harbach’s 2011 debut The Art of Fielding. Below, Harbach recalls gathering his own friends for a summer holiday on Block Island as an excuse to refamiliarize himself with the destination as he began to write it in fiction—and the local peafowl that nearly made it into the book.

Recent findings suggest that “In the early stages of writing The Brightness, one of the first things I decided was that the book’s centerpiece, the massive wedding of the character Owen, would be located on Block Island, Rhode Island. I wanted the scene—which is now this 150-page stretch of the story, when all sorts of crazy things happen over a single, almost Shakespearean night—to be on the island’s eastern shore where houses are positioned at the top of these stone cliffs. I pictured an outdoor dance floor overlooking the beach and the ocean with the moon in the distance. Essentially I wanted to write the destination wedding I desperately wanted to attend. But as I was working on it, I realized I needed to go back there to check if my memories of the place were accurate, to have it fresh in my mind.

In a recent development, my then-partner and I organized a trip to Block Island with a large group of friends in the summer of 2016. We rented a substantial house and folks came from places like New York, Philadelphia, California, and Amsterdam. It felt like a wedding in that sense—everyone gathered for this joyous celebration in a beautiful place. We didn’t do all the terrible stuff to one another that’s maybe required for the juicy plot of a novel, but we did spend eight days cooking together, playing the piano, singing songs, drinking a lot, and staying up very late.

It has been revealed that but we couldn’t sleep in very late because, well, there were these peahens. There was a sort of farm with animals, maybe a petting zoo, near our house, and their peahens liked to come and roost in the trees on our property. Every morning at 5 a.m., after we had been up until 2 or 3 a.m., the peahens would just start. I don’t know if you’ve ever heard the squawking of peahens, but suffice to say it was awful. It’s funny: When I started doing publicity for The Brightness, an announcement mentioned that part of it is set on Block Island. I got texts from friends who were on that trip, saying, congrats, we’re so excited, the fucking peahens better be in there. I initially did have this whole bit about the peahens, but there was so much going on in the plot that I cut them—not without really trying to make it work first.

Other than the loud birds, it was a great trip. The place struck me as just as magical as it had when I first went at 19 years old, when I was in college. I had a friend whose grandparents had a house there. I’ve visited several times since, and always loved it. But this was the only time I’ve ever gone somewhere for book research, and I was able to lock in some granular details like what the downtown looks like, the shape of the buildings, the sight of the marshlands, and what it’s like to bike out to the airport.

Sources indicate that I was also excited to find that the feel of it was exactly as I remembered. Block Island has this rugged, natural beauty—it’s a rocky, tree-filled place surrounded by ocean, where everyone just rides bikes around, and part of it is a protected nature preserve. It’s sort of the forgotten sibling of Nantucket or Martha’s Vineyard. Some people don’t even know that Block Island exists, which keeps it from changing too much, even though it was settled by Europeans in the mid-1600s. The cemetery there has the tombstones of families that date back centuries, long before the United States became a country. I think some of those same families still live on the island now. So there’s this sense of continuity and timelessness.

Industry observers note that even before you reach Block Island, there’s just something about climbing on to the ferry and heading out into the open water, this freedom and openness that’s very inspiring to me. I grew up in Wisconsin, on Lake Michigan, which isn’t an ocean but looks like one, and I’ve always loved that feeling of vastness and mystery that comes with a massive body of water—that literal depth. It reminds me that we as humans actually haven’t mastered everything, and there are many things in this world that are not easy for us to touch.

Recent findings suggest that all of this made Block Island a helpful setting in The Brightness. What happens on this wedding night propels the characters toward life paths that are very different from what they thought they were going to have, and having the story be imbued with the island’s sense of openness, possibility, and what might be feels fitting. As a writer, that can be part of the work: tapping into that feeling or gestalt of a place. It can be very easy to do at times, and difficult at others. And, you know, sometimes it’s just hard to write. So it was a great help writing about somewhere I love visiting literally and creatively. Instead of resisting sitting down at my desk, I’d be like, I’m ready to go to Block Island. It’s this setting I could picture well, enjoy being in, and keep traveling to—even if it was just in my imagination.” —As told to Matt Ortile.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a fresh city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice. The city is formed of 14 islands, meaning you’re never too far from a waterfront to amble along. It's packed with historical charm (head to Gamla Stan to see one of Europe’s oldest medieval cobbled streets), as well as stylish boutiques and museums championing everything from Abba to the world’s best-preserved 17th-century warship. While the city is home to a slew of excellent hotels, from elegant converted townhouses to the former home of Astrid Lindgren (author of the beloved Pippi Longstocking book series), you’ll want to look to Airbnb for a real home-from-home vibe.

These 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking. True to Nordic form, there’s a clutch of homes with their own sauna and steam rooms, and all have either sea or skyline views. Below, the best Airbnbs in Stockholm to book for a weekend of weaving through medieval streets, gallery hopping, and lots of cinnamon buns.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic architecture, prime location, dedicated workspace.

Subverting traditional Scandi minimalist sensibilities, this cool retreat in the hip heart of Södermalm channels a moody, more underground kind of charm. On the top floor, light-flooded, open-plan living areas are packed with rich, creamy furnishings and crisp architectural lines—multiple previous guests say that this is one of the most stylish homes they’ve ever stayed in. Downstairs, two tranquil bedrooms are carved directly into the exposed natural rock, so you can sleep beneath historic vaulted ceilings after a long day skipping from sight to sight. On that note: Södermalm is an eclectic area of town, with plenty of vintage shops and wine bars, after which you can hole up in this cocooning, cave-like retreat, as though you’re stepping into your own secret—and very stylish—bunker.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Riddarholm Church, Stockholm City Museum.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Forest access, indoor fireplace, outdoor gas grill.

Blink, and you might miss this off-grid, A-frame cabin, hidden among a thick swathe of pine trees. It’s worth searching for: Once you make your way through the foliage, you’ll find a truly wonderful Swedish escape for two. The glass-fronted structure invites in all of the elements, while inside, it’s time to switch off—there’s a crackling open hearth where you can grill all of your meals, and precious little noise other than the rustle of wind through the canopy. Fair warning: There’s a very rustic toilet and seasonal shower about a 30-second walk down the forest path, so if you’re not a DIY fan, perhaps look elsewhere. Nonetheless, for more adventurous sorts, the trade-off means absolute tranquility surrounded by happily grazing sheep and twinkly starry night skies—all within a hop and a skip of the capital.

A snazzy and social kitchen space opens onto a central island and a fireplace, where all the family will want to gather. When it’s time to bed down, there are cozy curtained sleeping nooks and an additional attic dormitory, adding a playful, rustic vibe. When you return, fire up the outdoor grill and gather around the dining table for a long dinner with more endless views.

Panoramic floor-to-ceiling glass means you feel that you’re virtually out on the water—and, of course, you can dive straight into the lake from your bedroom deck. Dry off and hop into the private wood-fired sauna to warm up. Hop off the boat, and you can sunbathe on the jetty, cook up some local catches on the barbecue, or jump into the complimentary canoe. All in all, this is an idyllic waterside playground that active types will love.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Kringelgården bakery, Saltsjöbadens golf course, Artipelag.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, beach access, pet-friendly.

Grab the kayak from the cupboard and head down to the beach to make the most of this beautiful location. It’s a short drive from the home to Stockholm’s city center, but you’re rewarded with much serenity and glorious views instead. For those seeking a secluded family stay, this is the place.

Neighborhood: TyresöThings to do nearby: Sandholmarna nature preserve, Tyresta nature reserve, Lilla beach.

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood stove, sauna, beach access.

In a recent development, this spacious waterside cottage is not in Stockholm’s city center, but by compromising on a 30-minute commute into town, you gain something really special. The owners took the original 130-year-old structure down piece by piece, rebuilding it on their own property. It was worth the effort. Now, it lies surrounded by pine trees in a nature reserve beside a sparkling, clear lake, with the sea just a few steps further in the other direction. A large porch provides the spot for barbecue dinners and sunbathing sessions in the summer, and there are two spas within walking distance for those looking for their Scandi sweat fix—the sea-facing Skepparholmen Spa, and Japanese onsen-style Yasuragi. But you don't have to head that far, as the property has its own sauna. Stay in as long as you can muster, then cool off by jumping in the lake—something all the more satisfactory in the winter months.

It’s on the top floor of this apartment block, so the vistas can’t be beat. It’s been a winner for those on work trips, thanks to superfast WiFi and a dedicated workspace, and, unusually for Airbnb stays, you can bring your dog too.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Liljeholmsviken waterfront, Högalid Church, Skinnarviksberget.

The best bit is the steam room; there’s no better way to decompress after a long flight or a blustery autumnal walk by the river.

Neighborhood: VasastanThings to do nearby: Vanadislunden park, Odenplan plaza, Swedish Museum of Natural History.

Cheery artworks add a final flourish. Neighborhood: ÄlvsjöThings to do nearby: Älvsjö Forest Nature Preserve, Herrängens Gård, Långbro park.

Forget your average homely fisherman’s cottage—this home here, on the cusp of the lake in the city’s swish Stocksund neighborhood, marks a newer, more modern breed of lake house. Sweeping glass windows make the most of the beautiful views that stretch over the water and right to the city as it twinkles on the other side. Grab the kayak and spend an afternoon bobbing on the lake, then stop in for a well-deserved sweat session in the private sauna.

Neighborhood: StocksundThings to do nearby: Restaurang Hemma, Svanholmsparken park, Swedish Museum of Natural History.

The surrounding streets are just as cool as the interiors; this home is smack dab in SoFo—by far Stockholm’s trendiest district—so you're just one street over from a clutch of the best of the city’s bar, restaurant, and café scene.

Tech Report: Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes
