    #7281. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (996 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., remarked, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it rapidly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, noted Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz mentioned that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    In a recent development, sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., stated after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    It has been revealed that for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., noted the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    Industry observers note that “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy mentioned, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford mentioned Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Bedford mentioned he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore newly introduced airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

    The Airbus A380 burns approximately 4,600 gallons (17,400 L) of fuel per hour. The Airbus A320 burns approximately 750 gallons (3,000 L). Framed as raw fuel consumption, the A380 uses roughly six times as much fuel as the A320, which is not a surprising difference, given that one is a 1,268,000-pound (575,000 kg), four-engine, double-deck widebody and the other is a 172,000-pound (78,000 kg), twin-engine narrowbody. The comparison becomes more interesting when the calculation accounts for how many passengers each aircraft carries per unit of fuel it burns.

    Recent findings suggest that per-passenger fuel efficiency is where the numbers shift, and where factors like seating configuration, load factor, and mission profile start to matter more than total fuel burn. An A380 carrying 615 passengers produces a very different per-passenger figure than one carrying 400 in a premium-heavy layout, and both look different from an A320 flying a two-hour domestic hop versus a four-hour cross-country route.

    The Airbus A380 burns approximately 4,600 gallons (17,400 L) per hour during cruise, powered by four Rolls-Royce Trent 900 or Engine Alliance GP7200 engines. At 10 gallons per nautical mile, it consumes more fuel per hour than any other commercial aircraft in service. The A380 carries up to 82,000 gallons (310,000 L) of fuel in its wing and fuselage tanks, enough to sustain flights of up to 8,000 nautical miles (14,800 km) at a cruise speed of Mach 0.85.

    The Airbus A320ceo burns approximately 750 gallons (2,840 L) per hour in cruise, powered by two CFM56 or IAE V2500 engines. The A320neo, equipped with CFM LEAP-1A or Pratt & Whitney GTF engines, reduces that figure to approximately 676 gallons (2,560 L) per hour, a 15-20% improvement over the older variant. The A320 carries approximately 6,300 gallons (24,200 L) of fuel, enough for its typical mission profile of 2-4 hour flights covering up to 3,300 nautical miles (6,100 km).

    The A380 burns roughly six times as much fuel per hour as an A320. That ratio reflects the difference in aircraft size, engine count, and mission. The A380's maximum takeoff weight is 1,268,000 pounds (575,000 kg). The A320's is approximately 172,000 pounds (78,000 kg). The A380 carries between 400 and 615 passengers depending on configuration. The A320 carries between 150 and 180. The raw fuel burn comparison is not useful on its own without accounting for how many passengers each aircraft carries on the fuel it consumes.

    Sources indicate that dividing each aircraft's fuel burn by its passenger count produces a comparison that looks very different from the raw hourly figures. The math is straightforward. The A380 burns approximately 8.2 gallons per statute mile at cruise. In a typical three-class configuration carrying 525 passengers, that works out to roughly 64 passenger-miles per gallon. In Emirates' higher-density 615-seat layout, the figure improves to approximately 75 passenger-miles per gallon.

    Sources indicate that the A320ceo burns approximately 1.45 gallons per statute mile at cruise. With 170 passengers on board, that produces roughly 117 passenger-miles per gallon. With 180 passengers in a higher-density layout, the figure rises to approximately 124. The A320neo, burning roughly 1.3 gallons per mile, pushes the number higher still, reaching approximately 130-138 passenger-miles per gallon depending on configuration.

    The A320 is the more fuel-efficient aircraft per passenger, and by a significant margin. A typical A320ceo delivers roughly 117 passenger miles per gallon compared to approximately 64-75 for the A380. The A320neo widens the gap further. The result may seem counterintuitive given the A380's scale, but the A320 benefits from having only two engines, a lighter airframe relative to its passenger count, and a more modern aerodynamic design in the NEO variant. The A380 spreads its fuel burn across more passengers than any other aircraft in service, but not enough to close the efficiency gap with a modern narrowbody.

    The per-passenger figures in the previous section assume every seat is occupied. In practice, no commercial flight operates at 100% load factor. The global average for international flights hovers around 82-85%, and individual flights vary widely depending on route, day of week, time of year, and market conditions. Load factor directly affects the per-passenger efficiency calculation because the aircraft burns the same amount of fuel regardless of how many seats are filled.

    An A380 configured with 525 seats at 85% load factor carries approximately 446 passengers. Its per-passenger efficiency drops from 64 passenger-miles per gallon to roughly 54. At a 70% load factor and carrying 368 passengers, the figure falls to approximately 45. Emirates operates its A380 fleet at consistently high load factors, often above 80%, which is part of why the aircraft remains economically viable for the airline. An operator running the same aircraft at a 65% load factor on a less-popular route would see per-passenger fuel efficiency deteriorate to levels that make the economics difficult to justify relative to a smaller widebody.

    The A320 follows the same math but starts from a higher baseline. At 85% load factor with 170 seats, the A320ceo carries 145 passengers and delivers roughly 100 passenger-miles per gallon. At 70%, carrying 119 passengers, the figure drops to approximately 82. Configuration matters independently of load factor. An A380 with a premium-heavy cabin carrying 400 passengers at full capacity produces worse per-passenger efficiency than the same aircraft configured with 615 economy seats at 80% load factor.

    The A380 and A320 operate on fundamentally different mission profiles, which affects how their fuel efficiency should be interpreted. Every flight includes a takeoff and climb phase that burns significantly more fuel per minute than cruise. On a two-hour A320 domestic flight, the takeoff and climb can account for 20-25% of the total fuel consumed. On a 14-hour A380 long-haul sector, the same phase represents a much smaller percentage of total burn because the aircraft spends the majority of its flight time at cruise altitude where fuel consumption per mile is lowest.

    Recent findings suggest that this means the A320's per-passenger efficiency on a short domestic sector is worse than its cruise-phase numbers suggest, while the A380's efficiency on a long-haul flight benefits from spending most of the mission at its most efficient operating point. A 90-minute A320 shuttle flight from New York to Washington burns more fuel per passenger-mile than the same aircraft flying a four-hour cross-country route, simply because the fuel-intensive takeoff and climb phase represents a larger share of the shorter mission.

    The two aircraft also serve different economic functions, making a direct efficiency comparison of limited practical value. Airlines do not choose between an A380 and an A320 for the same route. The A380 exists to move 500-plus passengers between major international hubs where demand justifies the capacity. The A320 is designed to carry 150-180 passengers on domestic and short-haul international routes where frequency matters more than size. Comparing their fuel efficiency is useful for understanding how aircraft size, engine count, and mission profile affect per-passenger consumption, but it does not represent a choice any airline actually faces.

    Sources indicate that both the A380 and the A320ceo are older-generation aircraft when measured against what is now available. The A350, which Airbus positions as the A380's effective successor on long-haul routes, achieves approximately 100 passenger-miles per gallon in a typical three-class configuration. That represents a roughly 30-50% improvement over the A380, depending on configuration and load factor, achieved through two engines instead of four, extensive composite construction, and Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines that are a full generation newer than those that power the A380. The Boeing 787 delivers similar per-passenger efficiency gains over the four-engine widebodies it was designed to replace.

    The A320neo improves on the A320ceo by 15-20% on a per-seat basis through its LEAP-1A or GTF engines and aerodynamic refinements, including sharklets. At approximately 130-138 passenger-miles per gallon, the A320neo is the most fuel-efficient narrowbody in its class. The A321neo and A321XLR push the family's efficiency further on longer routes where cruise represents a larger share of total fuel burn. The 737 MAX family offers comparable improvements over the 737NG generation.

    Recent findings suggest that the generational gap between the A380 and the aircraft replacing it is larger than the gap between the A320ceo and the A320neo. The A380 is being overtaken by aircraft that carry fewer passengers but burn so much less fuel per seat that the total operating economics favor the smaller aircraft on all but the highest-demand routes. The A320ceo is being replaced by a direct successor that does the same job more efficiently on the same routes.

    JetBlue is growing its presence in Central America and the Caribbean.

    For the first time ever, the carrier will serve the Honduran capital of Tegucigalpa. Starting Feb. 25, 2027, flights from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, will arrive at Palmerola International Airport in Comayagua, which serves Tegucigalpa.

    Currently, JetBlue’s only destination in Honduras is San Pedro Sula, in the country’s northwest.

    Industry observers note that on Feb. 23, the carrier will launch service between Fort Lauderdale and George Town, Grand Cayman, in the Cayman Islands.

    Both routes will operate daily, using a mix of Airbus A320 and A220 aircraft.

    It has been revealed that jetBlue will also offer limited-time daily service from Fort Lauderdale to Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, between Jan. 29 and Feb. 15. The connection will help travelers reach the islands during Carnival, the airline remarked.

    “We’re grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we’re committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they’re looking for,” Daniel Shurz, JetBlue’s senior vice president of revenue, network, and enterprise planning, mentioned in a news release. “With new international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we’re strengthening Fort Lauderdale’s role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean, making it easier for customers to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and travel across our growing network.”.

    American has prioritized Latin America as demand from U.S. markets, especially Miami, grows. The carrier just recently debuted service to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia and will add Barcelona, Venezuela, to its network in January.

    • Sources indicate that southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific.
    • Industry observers note that the agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S.
    • French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers announced a new interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

    Industry observers note that the agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

    French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

    Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

    French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

    Sources indicate that southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

    For French Bee customers, the new arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

    The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

    Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

    According to recent reports, senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a newly introduced majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    It has been revealed that “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting remarked the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    Recent findings suggest that that was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    In a recent development, “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., stated Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    According to recent reports, “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    It has been revealed that sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    It has been revealed that sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the newly introduced people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    Sources indicate that “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., stated Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the latest ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve noted many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    Recent findings suggest that that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who mentioned he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    In a recent development, kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    Recent findings suggest that “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    According to recent reports, “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    It has been revealed that sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but mentioned, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    In a recent development, “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he noted. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    According to recent reports, “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    In a recent development, “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    In a recent development, sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., stated, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why The Airbus A350-1000 Is The Only Jet That Can Fly Sydney To London Nonstop

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Qantas is gearing up to launch the world’s longest-ever commercial service between Sydney and London At 9,188 nautical miles (10,573 miles or 17,016 km) and scheduled to exceed 20 hours, the nonstop journey linking the Australian city and English capital will far outdo anything attempted by an airline before.
    • Sources indicate that the Airbus A3350-100ULR (Ultra Long Range) will be used as a result, having been developed specifically for the task.
    • Tweaks have been made to the existing Airbus A3501000 in order to bring the aircraft up to standard for the extreme distance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Qantas is gearing up to launch the world’s longest-ever commercial service between Sydney and London At 9,188 nautical miles (10,573 miles or 17,016 km) and scheduled to exceed 20 hours, the nonstop journey linking the Australian city and English capital will far outdo anything attempted by an airline before. But such an undertaking is no mean feat, and is something that cannot simply be served by any old aircraft.

    Sources indicate that the Airbus A3350-100ULR (Ultra Long Range) will be used as a result, having been developed specifically for the task. Qantas ordered 12 of these from Airbus in May 2022 under its “Project Sunrise” proposal to begin flying direct routes from Sydney Airport (SYD) to both Upcoming York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and London Heathrow Airport (LHR). Expectations are presently for the first of these to arrive next April, leaving the inaugural record-breaking flight at some point later in the year.

    Tweaks have been made to the existing Airbus A3501000 in order to bring the aircraft up to standard for the extreme distance. Though the conventional -1000 is impressive in itself, a 9,000-nautical-mile (10,357-mile or 16,668-km) range leaves its capabilities just shy of those needed for the ambitious connection.

    Industry observers note that besides structural improvements and reinforced landing gear to allow for an increased maximum take-off weight (MTOW), an extra rear center tank has been permanently fitted to the -1000ULR. The addition of this tank marks the most significant change between the duo. Able to hold 5,283 (US) gallons (20,000 liters), it takes the -1000ULR’s usable fuel capacity to 48,893 gallons (185,076 liters), according to airport and maintenance planning documents from Airbus.

    Select Airbus A350 XWB passenger variant specifications:.

    Approx range (nautical miles/km).

    Usable fuel capacity (Gallons/liters).

    Recent findings suggest that additional fuel capacity, naturally, translates to extended range. In the case of the -1000ULR, the extra tank allows distances of up to 9,800 nautical miles (11,278 miles or 18,150 km) to be flown. It is, by design, perfect for the Sydney and London link thanks to this additional fuel capacity, building on the already strong range boasted by the -1000.

    In a recent development, behind the -1000ULR’s boosted range is not just extra fuel capacity, however. In order to make nonstop flights between London and Sydney a reality, concessions have also been required elsewhere. Namely, Qantas’ -1000ULRs are set to have far fewer seats onboard than other Airbus A350 variants.

    Recent findings suggest that where the -1000 typically carries between 350 and 410 passengers in a three-class configuration, Qantas is poised to operate its -1000ULRs with 238 seats in a four-class layout. The difference is pretty stark, especially when you consider that the -1000 can carry up to a maximum of 480 people if needed.

    Qantas A350-1000ULR specifications:.

    According to recent reports, the key reason for this is weight. The -1000ULR has been designed for endurance, while the -1000 was developed with both range and seating in mind. Singapore Airlines, which currently operates the world’s longest route between the Asian city-state and New York, has made the same trade-off with the Airbus A350-900ULR. Here, the specialized variant carries 161 passengers against the 300 to 350 of its counterpart, the Airbus A350-900.

    Industry observers note that realistically, reduced capacity is probably not something Qantas executives will be overly worried about. Instead, the carrier should find itself able to charge a premium given both the lower availability of tickets, but more importantly, because of the time that can be shaved off the journey by avoiding a stop.

    Sources indicate that A good example is Singapore Airlines, which is the sole operator of the -900ULR. With no other nonstop services using ultra-long-haul aircraft available between Singapore and Fresh York, the airline has found itself operating alone at arguably the most premium end of the market. One can opt for the shorter journey time, but it will cost them. In this regard, it is no surprise that Singapore operates its -900ULRs with no basic economy seats.

    Industry observers note that for Qantas, the goal of linking Australia’s east coast and England’s capital equates to “a fresh dawn of travel” and the “final frontier of aviation” in its own words. Time will tell if the demand for an uninterrupted connection between the two is really there. But up until now, the hub-and-spoke model appears to have served passengers making the journey pretty well. Indeed, the flight is set to be such an undertaking that Qantas will offer an onboard “wellness zone” to “promote movement” during the near day-long amount of time passengers will spend in the air.

    The dominant reason the -1000ULR is the only jet that can make it between Sydney and London without stopping is that Boeing, whether intentionally or not, has not developed its own equivalent. Issues at the US plane maker have been well documented in recent years, most recently in terms of the heavily delayed Boeing 777X program.

    But despite being Boeing’s latest addition to its widebody portfolio, even the 777X will not match the -1000, let alone the -1000ULR, on range. Per Boeing, the 777-8 and 777-9 will be able to fly 8,745 nautical miles (10,064 miles or 16,200 km) and 7,285 nautical miles (8,383 miles or 13,500 km) respectively. This means neither will be close to being capable of making the journey that the -1000ULR is designed for. That said, each offers advantages in terms of capacity and payload against the A350 and, in particular, -1000ULR, so the argument is that they have been developed for a different purpose.

    According to recent reports, this differing design philosophy stretches to the Boeing 787, too. While the Dreamliner made regular nonstop flight between Australia and the United Kingdom possible, the -1000ULR has promised to go a step further. Qantas began flying between Perth and London in 2018 thanks to the 787, but the family's maximum 7,865-nautical-mile (9,050-mile or 14,570-km) range has meant a trip significantly further down under from London has always been out of question.

    It has been revealed that as it stands, an unbroken connection between Australia's east and England’s capital remains theoretical. Qantas has planned to start the service for several years, but delays have pushed the inaugural flight further and further back. News of the most recent delay struck earlier this month, placing the first trip somewhere towards the back end of 2027.

    According to Qantas, the first of its -1000ULRs was in the paint shop in Toulouse getting made up in the airline’s colors as of late May. Test flights were mentioned to be “just weeks away” at the time, with pilot training also “well underway” at Qantas’ newly introduced A350 simulator in Sydney.

    In the statement shared with Simple Flying, Qantas added: “Next month we'll announce the first route and timing of our inaugural commercial services [...] When these services take off, passengers will save up to four hours off the journey. Three aircraft are needed to run a daily non-stop service on either route [to Newly introduced York or London]. While the first aircraft delivery has shifted to April 2027, the next four will follow in quick succession, putting us back on our original schedule by November.”.

    According to recent reports, airbus’ A350 program was born out of the idea that ultra-long-haul was the next frontier in commercial aviation. The 1000ULR has looked to take this a step further. But, Qantas and Airbus have made a bet with the -1000ULR that passengers will be prepared to sit aboard an aircraft for potentially well over 20 hours at a time. Those who have made the trek from London to Sydney might tell you that the journey feels almost endless at the moment. Perhaps the roughly four hours of travel time the nonstop service will cut may make all the difference.

    Sources indicate that peers will be waiting in the wings to gauge Qantas' success, therefore, and whether the -1000ULR's popularity takes off should be revealed through appetite for the Sydney to London or New York connections. Experience would suggest that a break on what would otherwise almost be a full day aboard an aircraft is a necessity for many. But there too, the experience can largely depend on the fare type and whether one is enjoying the bells and whistles of premium service or is crammed into economy class.

    In a recent development, so, would you be keen to make the crossing in one fell swoop aboard a Qantas A350-1000ULR? Or, is the prospect of a 20-plus hour nonstop flight just too awful to bear? Feel free to let us know below.

    #7268. Tech Report: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (789 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that former Alaska Rep.
    • Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen.
    • In a recent development, the Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    Sources indicate that former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    In a recent development, the Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola stated in a statement after the race was called.

    Industry observers note that the Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    Recent findings suggest that she entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The Newly introduced York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has mentioned she had no connection to the scheme.

    Sources indicate that prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Industry observers note that trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    According to recent reports, the Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    Sources indicate that "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer stated in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    Industry observers note that in other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    In a recent development, the race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

    • Lufthansa Group aims to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa Group aims to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

    According to recent reports, the airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

    Company leaders mentioned their 2024 turnaround plan, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

    “The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action, and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter remarked.

    Lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

    Industry observers note that lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

    According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s a place for realpolitik in American foreign policy, but it needs to be based on a correct appraisal of our interests.
    • President Trump’s policy toward the Ukraine war has the trappings of realism yet is too personal and too hostile to an embattled ally to constitute a true exercise in hardheadedness.

    I’ve never flown Hawaiian Airlines — so why did I get its credit card?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I encourage travelers to think outside the box when it comes to the credit cards in their wallet.
    • It has been revealed that that rings true for me with the Hawaiian Airlines® World Elite Mastercard®.
    • The information for the Hawaiian Airlines World Elite Mastercard has been collected independently by The Points Guy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I encourage travelers to think outside the box when it comes to the credit cards in their wallet. Just because a card doesn't seem like a fit for you on the surface doesn't mean that's actually the case.

    It has been revealed that that rings true for me with the Hawaiian Airlines® World Elite Mastercard®. I've never flown with Hawaiian Airlines and don't have any concrete prepares to in the near future, yet this card offers significant value to me.

    Let me walk through exactly why that is.

    The information for the Hawaiian Airlines World Elite Mastercard has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

    The Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard earns Atmos Rewards points, which can be redeemed for Hawaiian, Alaska, Oneworld and nonalliance partner flights. As someone who was declined for the earlier this year, I didn't have a great way to earn Atmos Rewards points prior to opening this card.

    It has been revealed that I'm based in the Pacific Northwest, so flights on Alaska Airlines are a common feature of my travel plans. While I can book these with my American Airlines AAdvantage miles, I don't want to put all my eggs in one loyalty program, since that leaves my rewards vulnerable to future devaluations and other negative program changes.

    The Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard offers a compelling, easy-to-earn welcome bonus:.

    On top of that, I'll earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible Hawaiian and Alaska purchases and 2 points per dollar spent on dining, gas and groceries.

    Without this card, my only way of earning Atmos Rewards points was via Bilt Points transferred from my Bilt account, which isn't a particularly efficient method.

    While this card's benefits are understandably focused on Hawaiian Airlines, there are ways to use them on Alaska flights, too. I'll receive two free checked bags whenever I'm flying either Hawaiian or Alaska as long as I book with my card, a nice perk considering mid-tier cards typically only offer your first checked bag free.

    Upon account opening, I became eligible for a one-time 50% companion discount for one round-trip main cabin fare between North America and Hawaii. This is redeemable on either Alaska or Hawaiian, but I must use it within 13 months of account opening.

    Some possible use cases I have in mind include inviting a friend to join me on a trip to Hawaii or offering it to them as a discount for a positioning flight to Hawaii and back as part of a larger Asia itinerary we take together.

    Recent findings suggest that each account anniversary, this card offers a $100 companion discount for a round-trip main cabin fare, also usable on Alaska or Hawaiian. Both discounts may be subject to additional terms.

    While it's unfortunate that these companion discounts are limited to travel between Hawaii and North America, it's not surprising considering this is a Hawaiian Airlines-branded card. It's a good incentive for me to finally start seriously considering some of the trips I've had on my list.

    The or its more affordable sibling, the , are likely better first choices for Alaska flyers — and possibly Hawaiian Airlines flyers as well.

    According to recent reports, both cards offer a more valuable free checked bag benefit, with the opportunity to check a free bag for yourself as well as up to six people on the same itinerary (when you pay with your card). You'll also get preferred boarding on both airlines, which the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard doesn't offer.

    The Summit comes with eight Alaska lounge passes every year, a big upside for those flying Alaska often enough to value lounge access. It also earns well on foreign purchases, earning 3 points per dollar spent.

    Unless you never fly Alaska Airlines and fly Hawaiian frequently, I recommend applying for one of these cards first. If you wind up getting declined, as I did, I'd consider the Hawaiian Mastercard as an alternative.

    Recent findings suggest that carefully planning your credit card strategy never loses its importance. As someone with a well-established roster of transferable rewards cards, I'm in a phase where I'm considering how cobranded cards can boost my travels.

    The Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard isn't the obvious choice on the surface, but the benefits and rewards it offers make a lot of sense for me as an Alaska Airlines flyer. If you're a Hawaiian Airlines fan or travel frequently with Alaska but are ineligible for one of its credit cards, the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard may be the right choice for you.

    To learn more, check out our full review of the Hawaiian Airlines Mastercard.

    #7261. Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (664 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Surprise: Aer Lingus Unveils First-Ever Premium Economy, Coming To 10 A330s

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype.
    • This is quite a major change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.
    • The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aer Lingus is getting on the premium economy hype. The Irish flag carrier has today announced it will introduce the cabin for the first time on 10 of its Airbus A330s, which will also feature latest business and economy cabins (the product won’t be coming to the Airbus A321LR/XLR fleet).

    This is quite a major change, and one that should give it a leg up in the highly competitive trans-Atlantic market.

    The cabin will feature just four rows with 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. That’s about average when compared to other premium economy cabins. The narrow fuselage of the A330 means there’s only room for three seats in the middle section, rather than the four many other airlines offer.

    According to recent reports, in terms of specs, the 18-19 inch wide Recaro R4 seats will offer 38 inches of pitch and eight inches of recline. In addition to footrests, a staple of any decent premium economy, the seats have been designed with fixed headrest wings to provide a sense of privacy.

    As for the soft product, Aer Lingus promises three-course dining, drinks throughout the flight, a pillow and blanket, an amenity kit, and noise-reducing (not noise-canceling) headphones.

    Sources indicate that I actually really like the design and color scheme. It’s modern, looks elegant and premium, and most importantly of all for the airline of the Emerald Isle, the colors are quintessentially Irish.

    Aer Lingus notes premium economy fares will start from 700 Euros one-way, putting a return trip at around 1,400 Euros. That works out to around $1,534, and a few hundred dollars cheaper than United’s nonstop fares from Newark (EWR) to Dublin (DUB).

    We’ll have to wait until October 1 next year to try Aer Lingus’ new premium economy out for ourselves. The airline hasn’t yet unveiled which routes will get the product first, but we should find out in the coming months.

    The good news is, they’ll operate on many of the airline’s 18 nonstop routes from Dublin to the United States.

    Sources indicate that as a small, almost boutique-style airline with just 63 aircraft, Aer Lingus must remain competitive, especially in the saturated transatlantic market in which it predominantly operates. The addition of premium economy bridges the large gap between economy and business, and should open the airline up to a potential upcoming customer base who’ve never flown it before.

    I’ll be attending an event in Dublin tonight, so I should be back with more images and extra info soon!

    What do you make of Aer Lingus’ new premium economy?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The rejections of Viktor Orbán and Donald Trump hold sobering lessons for the nationalist right.

    On Election Night this past May in Budapest, I was in the ballroom when a defining political era ended faster than it takes to place a drink order at a party-district ruin bar on a Saturday night. Viktor Orbán, the four-term prime minister who for 16 years was the undisputed sovereign of Hungarian politics, and the monster that haunted the nightmares of globalists from Brussels to Washington, took the stage not long after election results began rolling in — and gracefully accepted defeat. It was as if magician David Copperfield had made the Matterhorn disappear before the audience settled into its chairs on the chalet lawn.

    Just like that, Orbán was gone. When I first arrived in Budapest for a fellowship in 2021, a Hungarian conservative friend told me that everybody knows Orbán’s Fidesz Party is riddled with corruption, but people tolerate it because life has been getting better and better for them since the reformist prime minister took power in 2010. “But if the economy ever turns,” he said, “then corruption is going to matter. A lot.”.

    Rod Dreher is the author of six books, including the New York Times bestsellers The Benedict Option (2017) and Live Not By Lies (2020).

    On “Is There Still Hope for Postliberalism?”.

  • Airline baggage fees in the U.S. have increased in 2026, with first checked bags typically starting around $45 to $50 each way and higher costs for additional or overweight bags.
  • Carry-on allowances vary, but most major airlines permit one personal item and one carry-on bag, with some low-cost carriers charging extra or imposing stricter limits.
  • Paying for baggage online in advance can reduce costs, and certain fare types or elite status may include free checked bags or higher weight limits.
  • There are multiple strategies to avoid or reduce baggage fees, including holding elite status, booking premium cabin tickets, or using specific travel benefits.
  • Baggage fees differ by airline, fare type, travel date and whether payment is made online or at the airport.
  • Low-cost carriers often have the highest and most variable fees, and may enforce stricter weight limits (e.g., 40 pounds for checked bags on some airlines).
  • Specialty items and overweight or oversized bags typically incur additional charges, and policies for basic economy fares can be more restrictive.

    • According to recent reports, it’s not just Aer Lingus’ premium economy stealing the headlines in Ireland today.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, it’s not just Aer Lingus’ premium economy stealing the headlines in Ireland today. Expected to fly passengers for the first time on October 1, 2027, the fresh cabins are part of a comprehensive Airbus A330 tip-to-tail retrofit that will include new business and economy cabins. We covered the premium economy cabin in a separate article story.

    In a recent development, the same 10 Airbus A330s that will get the airline’s latest premium economy will also get a swanky new business class. The airline’s Airbus A321XLRs aren’t included in this cabin update.

    Aer Lingus opted for its take on the ever-popular Collins Elevation suite. There’ll be 28 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration that stretch out to 78 inches long when in lie-flat mode.

    According to recent reports, the color palette of Irish greens, whites, and light wood gives the seat an elegant yet distinctly non-corporate feel. It’s a thumbs-up from me.

    In terms of updated tech, each seat has 4K HD screens (in all cabins) as well as wireless and USB-C charging. While nothing revolutionary, these touches will significantly modernize Aer Lingus A330 cabins.

    According to recent reports, aer Lingus is also introducing a self-service bar stocked with snacks and drinks. I wonder if this will include Champagne….

    The airline will also serve up a whole new in-flight dining experience featuring dishes inspired by both Irish ingredients and its transatlantic destinations.

    It wouldn’t be a full retrofit without sprucing up economy.

    Per the renderings, Aer Lingus has done a great job again with the cabin’s look and feel. The emerald green Shamrocks are a lovely touch.

    Seats are configured in the A330’s classic 2-4-2 configuration — a favorite for those traveling in pairs.

    While the recline looks a bit modest here, the seat’s thickness looks like it’ll provide more support than some of those ultra-thin, rigid seats airlines are sneaking in these days.

    The six-way adjustable headrests should also mean less head-wobbling when catching some shut-eye.

    The curved design of the seat backs should hopefully mean noticeably more knee space.

    Industry observers note that aer Lingus is also upping its food and beverage ante for economy passengers. In addition to a snack bar, a fresh mid-flight snack will be offered.

    A retrofit program like this was essential for Aer Lingus to remain competitive in the transatlantic market. The introduction of premium economy was a great move, especially since the cabin is known to be highly profitable.

    Recent findings suggest that aer Lingus has also done a great job of matching the Irish color scheme and sleek design across all cabins, which is more than can be said for some airlines these days. 😉.
